strengths: Addresses an important, high-stakes gap: realistic open-ended mental-health QA is substantially more informative than exam-style medical QA.

COUNSELBENCH-EVAL represents substantial data-collection effort. It uses 100 practitioners, five ratings per response, source-blinded and randomized presentation, a human-therapist baseline, and both span annotations and written rationales.
The within-question design, where the same raters assess all four response sources, supports comparatively controlled paired analysis.

The two benchmark components are complementary: naturalistic questions characterize typical behavior, while clinician-authored prompts attempt targeted stress testing across multiple model families and generations.

The appendices provide useful detail on prompts, question selection, annotator backgrounds, compute, and secondary analyses; the observed divergence between expert and LLM-judge ratings is practically relevant.
weaknesses: The central COUNSELBENCH-ADV results lack reliable ground truth. GPT-4.1 labels all 3,240 responses, while only 96 responses—about 3%—are checked by a single clinician, obtaining just 72.9% raw agreement. There is no random/stratified sampling description, chance-corrected agreement, per-failure confusion matrix, or precision/recall analysis. This is insufficient to support Table 3's model comparisons.

There is no matched non-adversarial control set or statistical testing for the adversarial results, so the paper cannot establish that the authored questions increase failure rates. Claims that failures are rooted in pretraining or exhibit clear family-level patterns are also unsupported causal or inferential conclusions.

The key Medical Advice construct conflates clinical content with unsafe or unauthorized advice. Models are explicitly prompted to act as professional therapists, and examples treat mentioning CBT or SSRIs—even alongside referral to a professional—as a safety failure. Conversely, licensed human therapists receive the highest flag rate. Thus the metric does not cleanly measure harm, appropriateness, or authorization.

Reliability evidence is incomplete and methodologically questionable. The paper averages per-question Krippendorff's alpha values computed from only four response units, reports no uncertainty, and omits Medical Advice merely because it is binary even though nominal alpha supports binary data. This leaves the principal safety outcome without demonstrated agreement.

The expert characterization is inconsistent: the contribution statement says 100 licensed professionals, whereas eligibility and Appendix B include trainees, associates, degree-only participants, and professionally trained individuals. Results are not separated by licensure, despite observed rating differences by experience.

Question selection introduces substantial scope and selection bias: only 100 highly upvoted questions are retained, one author subjectively replaces controversial or uncomfortable cases, and LGBTQ, sexuality, intimacy, spirituality, and religion topics are excluded. The benchmark also lacks deliberate crisis and self-harm coverage, limiting broad claims about mental-health safety and representativeness.

The LLM-judge span analysis reports only brittle exact/containment-based recall against a weak threshold of two out of five annotators, without precision or false-positive analysis. The thematic analysis is likewise ultimately labeled by GPT-4.1 without reported validation.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting are insufficient: several API model snapshots and access dates are unspecified, generation seeds are absent despite being claimed, model-dependent 250-word rejection sampling is unquantified, confidence intervals/effect sizes and multiple-testing corrections are missing, and the claimed public data/code release has no location in the manuscript.

Ethical reporting is incomplete. The approving institution is left blank, annotator compensation is not disclosed, and the discussion does not address contextual privacy or consent concerns around republishing sensitive public mental-health narratives. Numerous presentation inconsistencies—such as eight versus nine LLM judges and an almost empty final page—further reduce polish.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, high-stakes gap: evaluating open-ended mental-health support rather than exam-style factual QA.

COUNSELBENCH-EVAL involves substantial expert data collection: 100 credential-checked practitioners, five source-blinded ratings per response, randomized within-question comparisons, and written rationales with span-level evidence.
The combination of naturalistic questions and 120 clinician-authored stress tests is potentially valuable, and the experiments cover multiple model families and generations.
The evidence that many LLM judges inflate scores and miss expert-flagged content is practically important. The appendix also provides useful prompts, generation settings, and annotator breakdowns.
weaknesses: The central safety construct lacks validity. “Medical Advice” measures whether content belongs within licensed practice, but the paper interprets this as harmful or “unauthorized” for models while comparing against licensed human authors. Examples classify hedged, factual discussion of SSRIs or CBT—and even stating that purging is unhealthy—as failures. No psychometric or prescriber-led consensus validation is presented.

COUNSELBENCH-ADV’s headline results rely almost entirely on GPT-4.1 labels. One clinician checked only 96 of 3,240 responses, obtaining 72.9% raw agreement; the sampling scheme, class prevalence, chance-corrected agreement, class-wise precision/recall, and adjudication are absent. This is insufficient to establish reliable ground truth.

There is no matched non-adversarial control, so the paper cannot show that its questions increase failure rates above ordinary base rates. The six modes are manually selected from a few model-specific examples, prompts are not independently validated, clustered generations are treated without uncertainty, and no significance tests or confidence intervals support the claimed family-level patterns. Failure of one few-shot configuration also does not imply that problems originate in pretraining.

The main model-human comparison is substantially confounded. CounselChat is public pre-2022 material with no contamination analysis; questions and human answers are selected through upvotes and manual filtering, while models answer a therapist-persona prompt; historical human responses are not elicited under matched conditions; and response-length distributions and regeneration counts are unreported. Consequently, LLaMA-3.3’s large apparent advantage over humans is difficult to interpret.

Statistical reporting is inadequate. Table 1 lacks uncertainty and effect sizes; numerous pairwise Wilcoxon tests have no multiplicity correction and do not model the crossed question/rater structure; Medical Advice receives no inferential test; and averaging per-question Krippendorff alpha values computed from only four response items is nonstandard and insufficiently explained.

The LLM-judge span experiment reports only recall-like exact/substring overlap, without precision or false-positive rates, and several denominators are very small. Table 14’s significance comparison is ambiguous, the text inconsistently says eight versus nine judges, and proprietary model snapshots are incompletely specified.

The scope is narrower than the claims suggest: EVAL contains only 100 highly curated questions and deliberately excludes LGBTQ, sexuality, and religion-related cases, with no crisis-handling, cultural-fairness, or subgroup analysis. Positioning against existing open-ended expert benchmarks such as HealthBench is also superficial.

Reproducibility and ethics reporting are incomplete: no accessible data/code artifact accompanies the stated release, exact clinician-authoring instructions are absent, annotator compensation is unreported, the approving IRB body is blank, and searchable re-identification or secondary-use risks for sensitive public posts are not addressed. Removing explicit identifiers and citing an MIT license do not fully resolve these concerns.

The human-evaluation effort is substantial. It covers 400 unique responses to 100 questions, with five ratings per response from 100 credential-checked or professionally trained annotators. Source blinding, randomized answer order, and using the same raters for all four answers to a question support paired comparisons.

The annotations are unusually rich, combining multidimensional scores, extracted spans, and written rationales. The appendix also provides useful transparency about credentials, survey prompts, model prompts, and response selection.

The comparison between human experts and nine LLM judges yields a practically important observation: most automated judges show severe score compression and very low sensitivity to expert-flagged medical advice, factual errors, and toxic content.

Expert-authored adversarial questions and multiple generations from nine model families constitute a potentially valuable stress-testing resource, provided its labels and failure taxonomy are strengthened.
weaknesses: COUNSELBENCH-EVAL has a serious contamination risk. The exact CounselChat questions and answers were publicly available before the evaluated models were trained, yet no memorization or decontamination analysis is reported. Moreover, only five questions per topic are retained through upvote-based and subjective manual selection, so the sample is neither random nor demonstrably representative despite broad claims about realistic mental-health QA.

The rubric has weak construct validity for a clinical benchmark. The actual survey gives only short, largely unanchored definitions for factual consistency and toxicity. “Medical advice” conflates prescribing, mentioning a therapy modality, general psychoeducation, and appropriately hedged referral; several supposedly problematic examples are professionally defensible. The models are explicitly instructed to act as “a professional therapist,” which induces the boundary-crossing behavior subsequently penalized, while the human comparison answers were written by actual therapists.

The central COUNSELBENCH-ADV results are not adequately validated. GPT-4.1 labels all 3,240 responses, while only 96 are spot-checked by one clinician, producing just 72.9% raw agreement. There is no chance-corrected agreement, uncertainty interval, stratification, or per-failure precision/recall. Errors of this magnitude can readily change the reported model rankings and trigger rates, making reliance on an LLM judge especially problematic given the paper’s own evidence that LLM judges miss clinical failures.

The adversarial taxonomy is narrow and subjective: six modes are selected as two examples associated with each of three initial models, apparently from one response and two comments per mode. There is no independent content-validity assessment, inter-rater verification of the 120 prompts, or confirmation that prompts uniquely target their assigned failure. Important risks such as crisis escalation, self-harm, privacy, bias, dependency, and fabricated resources are absent.

Claims from the adversarial experiments exceed the evidence. There are no confidence intervals or statistical tests for model-family patterns or zero-shot/few-shot differences, despite clustering by question author, question, and three repeated generations. The few-shot demonstrations are generic high-rated answers rather than targeted counterexamples; their limited effect cannot establish that failures are “rooted in pretraining.”

The statistical treatment needs substantial revision. The effective primary sample is 100 questions and 400 responses, not 2,000 independent examples. Averaging separately computed Krippendorff alpha values over questions containing only four answer units is insufficiently justified, and uncertainty intervals are absent. No multiple-comparison correction is reported, categorical medical-advice differences are not tested despite being a headline result, and ancillary analyses ignore annotator/question clustering.

The LLM-judge conclusions are partly overstated. All nine judges and the experts rank LLaMA-3.3 highest on overall quality, while the emphasized GPT-4/Gemini inversion concerns expert means of 3.28 versus 3.26 that are explicitly nonsignificant (p=0.72). The paper reports aggregate means rather than item-level agreement, calibration, or rank correlations; its sentence analysis measures exact-match recall only, without precision. Human raters also provide rationales and evidence spans whereas LLM judges are instructed to return scores without explanation, confounding the comparison.

Generation and baseline choices limit fairness and reproducibility. COUNSELBENCH-EVAL uses only one stochastic output per model and repeatedly resamples model answers until they fit 250 words, a model-dependent selection process that reportedly takes days in some cases. Exact API revisions, query dates, generation seeds, rejection counts, and several model identifiers are missing. Historical forum answers are not a controlled human baseline, and the promised data/code release is not linked in the manuscript.

Generalizability and ethics are underdeveloped. The study excludes LGBTQ, sexuality, spirituality, and religious topics and does not cover suicide/self-harm, while 75% of annotators are White, 84% are female, and all recruitment is U.S.-based; no subgroup analysis or user/patient evaluation is provided. The ethics statement mentions exempt review and de-identification but not annotator compensation, protections from distressing material, or the limits of treating a public-data license as user consent. Numerous presentation inconsistencies—eight versus nine judges, incorrect figure/table references, an incomplete related-work sentence, and an ambiguous Table 14 caption—further reduce confidence. Overall, the expert dataset is promising, but these validity problems affect the central benchmark and adversarial claims, placing the submission below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

Several analyses depend on automated labels without adequate validation. The paper demonstrates that GPT-4.1 is a weak failure detector (F1 approximately 0.49), yet subsequently uses it to evaluate the few-shot and domain-specific experiments. The large discrepancies between expert rates in Table 3 and GPT-4.1-derived rates in Table 17 undermine those results, and the conclusion that failures reflect “pretraining-level limitations” is unsupported.

The reliability and statistical analyses need strengthening. Averaging per-question Krippendorff alpha values computed from only four response items is nonstandard and unstable; uncertainty intervals, effect sizes, hierarchical analyses, and multiple-comparison corrections are absent. The qualitative GPT-4.1 coding also lacks validation against the researchers’ manual codes.

Exact API snapshots/dates, generation seeds, rejection counts, response-length distributions, and clearer handling of abstentions are needed for reproducibility. Several reporting descriptions also risk overstating the evidence, particularly the implication that five experts rated every adversarial output.

COUNSELBENCH-EVAL represents substantial data-collection effort: 100 credential-checked practitioners, blinded and randomized presentation, five ratings per response, paired evaluation of all four sources for each question, and accompanying spans and rationales.
Combining evaluations of naturally occurring questions with targeted stress tests is potentially useful, as is directly examining whether LLM judges reproduce expert judgments.
The appendices provide model prompts, generation settings, annotator demographics, survey interfaces, qualitative examples, and several supplementary analyses.
weaknesses: The central constructs are insufficiently validated. The actual survey provides brief questions rather than operational definitions or calibration examples, and there is no reported content-validity study or patient-stakeholder input. Several purported failures are clinically contestable: responsibly mentioning CBT or SSRIs is treated as unauthorized advice, while describing purging as unhealthy is used to define a judgmental response. Consequently, the reported safety rates do not reliably measure harmfulness or clinical inappropriateness.

COUNSELBENCH-ADV has 1,080 responses and only 1,080 human labels distributed across five experts, apparently leaving each response singly annotated. There is no human-human reliability or adjudication for these subjective labels. With only 20 questions per failure mode, one stochastic response per model-question, and no confidence intervals or significance tests, the model- and family-level conclusions are fragile.

The six adversarial failure modes are hand-selected—two examples associated with each of three initial models—rather than derived through a validated or comprehensive taxonomy. There is no matched natural-question control demonstrating that the prompts increase failure rates, and some intended failures occur rarely or not at all. Claims that the benchmark effectively triggers failures and reveals stable family-level patterns are therefore overstated.

The LLM-judge analysis relies heavily on differences in average scores and rankings over only four response sources, without adequate item-level agreement, calibration, or discrimination analysis. Its span experiment reports recall-like detection rates but not precision, uses small consensus sets and brittle sentence matching, and does not establish that the human spans themselves are reliable.

The paper subsequently uses GPT-4.1 as the judge for the few-shot and domain-model analyses even though its own adversarial evaluation reports only 0.49 F1 against the single-expert labels. The conclusion that minimal few-shot improvement implies a pretraining-level limitation is especially unsupported by this unreliable measurement and does not follow causally from the experiment.

System comparisons contain major confounds. LLM outputs are repeatedly regenerated until shorter than 250 words, whereas human answers are filtered and selected from an upvote-driven forum; response lengths and regeneration counts are not reported. The models are also instructed to impersonate a professional therapist. These choices can strongly affect specificity, perceived quality, and advice frequency, so rankings—particularly the surprising comparison with human therapists—cannot be cleanly attributed to model quality.

The statistical treatment is incomplete. Krippendorff's alpha is described as averaged over questions, apparently using only four response units per question, without sufficient computational detail or uncertainty. Numerous pairwise tests lack multiplicity correction and effect sizes, and the time- and experience-based analyses do not account for repeated ratings nested within annotators and questions.

Scope and representativeness are overstated: the primary set contains only 100 English, single-turn, upvote-selected questions; annotators are U.S.-based and demographically concentrated; and LGBTQ, sexuality, religion, spirituality, and other sensitive topics are deliberately excluded despite their importance in mental health. There is no dedicated limitations section.

Reproducibility is asserted rather than demonstrated: no accessible data or code artifact is identified, exact versions or access dates are missing for several API models, generation seeds and rejection-sampling counts are absent, and subjective manual question replacements are not enumerated.

The ethics discussion is too brief for releasing verbatim, highly sensitive mental-health posts. Dataset licensing and removal of explicit identifiers do not eliminate search-based re-identification or contextual-consent risks, and the paper does not discuss safeguards for annotators exposed to self-harm, abuse, and eating-disorder content.

COUNSELBENCH-EVAL represents substantial data-collection effort: 100 credential-checked practitioners, blinded and randomized response presentation, five ratings per response, multiple dimensions, span annotations, and written rationales.
The combination of real forum questions, a human-response baseline, clinician-authored adversarial prompts, and evaluations of several model families could become a useful community resource.
The manuscript is generally clear and supplies extensive appendices covering prompts, annotator backgrounds, selection procedures, computational resources, and additional analyses.
weaknesses: The central safety interpretation is conceptually problematic. The rubric asks whether content constitutes advice that should be given by a licensed professional, while models are explicitly prompted to act as professional therapists and human answers actually come from therapists. Because raters are source-blind, this measures the presence of professional-type advice—not whether it is unauthorized, unsafe, improperly qualified, or harmful. Consequently, conclusions about “unauthorized medical advice” are not supported by the measurement.

COUNSELBENCH-ADV does not establish an adversarial effect because it has no matched ordinary-question control or baseline failure rate. Moreover, Appendix H indicates that the 1,080 responses are distributed across five evaluators rather than independently rated by all five, and no human-human reliability is reported; agreement with GPT-4.1 is not a substitute, especially when the paper itself finds LLM judges unreliable. The claimed model-family patterns also lack uncertainty estimates or statistical tests.

The main comparison has substantial uncontrolled confounding. It uses one stochastic generation per model and question, compares differently aged models, does not match response lengths within the 250-word cap, and contrasts prompted model answers with organically written forum answers. Blinding does not prevent source inference from style and verbosity. No sensitivity analysis tests these factors.

All questions and human answers come from a public pre-2022 corpus that may be present in model training data, yet there is no contamination or answer-overlap analysis. Selecting highly upvoted, short-answer questions, manually replacing uncomfortable cases, and excluding areas such as sexuality, LGBTQ topics, and religion further limits representativeness—particularly for a mental-health safety benchmark.

The statistical treatment is insufficient for several headline conclusions: the paper reports no confidence intervals or effect sizes, does not correct numerous pairwise tests, performs no inference for Medical Advice, and averages per-question Krippendorff alpha values apparently computed from only four response units each. A crossed or mixed-effects analysis accounting for questions and annotators would be more appropriate.

The LLM-judge analysis on COUNSELBENCH-EVAL focuses largely on aggregate means rather than per-response calibration, ordinal agreement, correlation, or ranking metrics. Its span analysis reports recall under brittle text matching without precision. The few-shot experiment then relies on GPT-4.1 as the sole judge despite its reported F1 of 0.49 and draws an unsupported causal conclusion about “pretraining-level limitations.”

Safety coverage is incomplete for the stated domain: crisis escalation, suicidality and self-harm handling, privacy, hallucinated resources, demographic bias, and appropriate refusal are not systematically evaluated. Toxicity and the problematic Medical Advice item do not adequately cover these risks.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the manuscript: the promised data and code have no accessible location, several proprietary-model snapshot identifiers and evaluation dates are missing, and generation seeds and rejection-sampling retry statistics are not reported. Sensitive public mental-health text also warrants a fuller discussion of indirect re-identification and original-user consent. These issues collectively keep an otherwise promising resource below the top-tier acceptance threshold.
